scenarios.title: Scope a keyboard layout to one Xorg device
scenarios.summary: Correct the language desk keyboard and keep the operator and spare keyboards on their existing layout.
scenarios.objective: Configure the supplied language desk for the French fr layout. Keep the operator and spare keyboards on their US us layout. Apply the configuration and verify the physical key probe for each device.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the failed requirement with what the virtual session, client or key trial actually shows.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: A display manager starts a graphical session after login. In a native Xorg session the X server handles display and input for applications. DISPLAY=:0 names the local display in this exercise. A native Wayland session uses a different configuration path.

guide.title: Try the separate example
guide.why: Each InputClass applies to input devices matching its conditions. MatchIsKeyboard "on" requires a keyboard. MatchProduct "Library desk" matches that literal substring in the product name. More than one class can match the same device.

guide.title: Complete the independent assignment
guide.why: A later matching class can override the layout set by a previous class. Verify that your targeted change takes effect and that the common setting remains active on the other keyboards.

scenarios.explanation: The narrow product match applies the French layout only to the intended device. The other keyboards retain the common US rule. The key probe tests the applied state.
hints: Compare the product names with the specific rule’s MatchProduct value.
A later matching rule can change a layout selected by an earlier rule. Inspect matched rule names under the probe.
The physical Q position produces a with the supplied French layout and q with US.
scenarios.simplifications: The workspace uses supplied desktop settings and short input or connection trials. It never starts a real display server, remotely connects, reads host keys, or changes desktop settings. The profile excludes X authentication, real protocol exchanges, full XKB maps, physical devices and real assistive tools.

scenarios.title: Choose a remote desktop arrangement
scenarios.summary: Let a staff observer view the existing demonstration and allow a separate employee to log in.
scenarios.objective: Allow the staff observer to view the existing demonstration without controlling it. Allow the employee to log in to a separate session. Use the compatible client and active port for each connection.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the failed requirement with what the virtual session, client or key trial actually shows.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: GNOME, KDE and Xfce are desktop environments. A remote protocol tells client and service how to communicate. The supplied GNOME profile uses RDP. Its RDP listener cannot accept a VNC-only client.

guide.title: Try the separate example
guide.why: Desktop Sharing makes the existing desktop available. View only permits observation. Allow input control also lets that client interact. Remote Login is for a separate account to log in.

guide.title: Complete the independent assignment
guide.why: In this profile Remote Login uses TCP 3389. Desktop Sharing uses TCP 3389 when it is on by itself. With both services enabled, sharing moves to TCP 3390. The supplied identity grants determine who may use each service.

scenarios.explanation: Sharing and remote login solve different requests. When both modes are active in this profile, their endpoints differ. Correct clients reach the intended service with the supplied grants.
hints: Observe means Desktop Sharing with View only. A new account session needs Remote Login.
With both services active, compare the shown sharing port with the observer’s selected port.
A VNC-only client cannot speak to either supplied RDP service.

scenarios.title: Configure an accessible input profile
scenarios.summary: Set up a virtual desk for readable text and reliable typing, then check the results on supplied samples.
scenarios.objective: Show the reading sample in large text and high contrast. Allow a separate Shift tap to apply to the next letter. Ignore the unintended rapid repeat while keeping short presses of different letters.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the failed requirement with what the virtual session, client or key trial actually shows.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Larger text and higher contrast are separate settings. Compare the reading sample with each active. A screen reader or refreshable Braille can provide access when the user needs to read without relying on the screen.

guide.title: Try the separate example
guide.why: Shift is a modifier that changes the next letter. In the simple Sticky Keys probe, tap and release Shift, then tap A. A following B is lowercase unless Shift is used again.

guide.title: Complete the independent assignment
guide.why: Slow Keys waits for each press to be held long enough. Bounce Keys can ignore rapid repeats of the same key. The probe shows the press time and duration so you can tell the two problems apart.

scenarios.explanation: The visual sample meets the reading request. Sticky Keys lets the operator press Shift separately, and the repeat filter rejects only the unintended second A in this supplied trace.
hints: Text size and contrast are independent settings in the reading sample.
Use Sticky Keys when pressing Shift and the letter together is impractical.
The mistake in this case is a repeat of the same key. Compare Slow Keys with Bounce Keys on the short intentional taps.
